title: Propositional Logic and Truth Tables
subtitle: How five little words let you check an argument like a machine
objectives: By the end you will be able to define the five standard connectives (not, and, or, if-then, if-and-only-if) and write their truth tables from memory.
By the end you will be able to use a truth table to test whether a short argument is valid.
By the end you will be able to recognize modus ponens, modus tollens and disjunctive syllogism, and explain why they always work.
By the end you will be able to spot the formal fallacies of affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent, and produce a counterexample row that exposes them.
By the end you will be able to explain the puzzles of the 'material conditional' and why logicians accept it anyway.
hook:
A detective says: "If the butler did it, there will be mud on his boots. There is mud on his boots. So the butler did it." Half the room nods. It sounds tidy, it sounds logical, and it is completely broken. The gardener could have borrowed those boots; the butler could have walked through a flowerbed on his way to church. The premises can both be true while the conclusion is false.

On Day 17 you met Aristotle's syllogisms, which reason about categories ("All humans are mortal"). Today you learn a different and in some ways more basic machine: **propositional logic**, which reasons about whole statements joined by little words like *and*, *or*, *not* and *if*. Its great gift is a mechanical test, the truth table, that settles questions like the detective's without any appeal to intuition. Once you have it, you will hear broken arguments everywhere.

sections.heading: Propositions and the Stoic Invention
sections.body:
A **proposition** is something that can be true or false: "It is raining," "Paris is in France," "The butler did it." Questions ("Is it raining?") and commands ("Shut the door!") are not propositions, because it makes no sense to call them true or false.

Propositional logic treats simple propositions as unbreakable atoms and gives each a capital letter: let P stand for "It is raining" and Q for "The streets are wet." Then it studies how atoms combine into compound propositions, like "If it is raining, then the streets are wet." The key insight is that the truth of a compound often depends *only* on the truth of its parts, not on what they are about. Such connectives are called **truth-functional**: feed in the truth values of the parts and the truth value of the whole pops out, like a function in mathematics.

Aristotle did not develop this kind of logic. The credit for its first systematic version goes to the Stoics you met on Day 25, above all Chrysippus (c. 279–206 BCE), who analyzed arguments built from "if," "and" and "or" and identified five "indemonstrable" argument forms that he took to be self-evidently valid. Sadly almost all his writings are lost and we know them through later summaries.

The subject was reborn in the nineteenth century. George Boole's *The Laws of Thought* (1854) showed that reasoning with "and," "or" and "not" could be treated as a kind of algebra, and Gottlob Frege (Day 69) built propositional logic into the foundation of his far more powerful system. The truth table as a visual tool was popularized in the early 1920s by Ludwig Wittgenstein (Day 70) and, independently, by Emil Post, though versions of the idea appear earlier, including in the work of C. S. Peirce (Day 67).

sections.heading: The Five Connectives and Their Truth Tables
sections.body:
Logicians use symbols so that the form of an argument stands out. Here are the five standard **connectives**, with the symbols you will most often see. A **truth table** lists every possible combination of truth values for the parts (T for true, F for false) and shows the value of the whole.

**Negation** (not), written ¬P. It simply flips the value.
- P is T: ¬P is F
- P is F: ¬P is T

**Conjunction** (and), written P ∧ Q. True only when both parts are true. The two parts are called **conjuncts**.
- P T, Q T: P ∧ Q is T
- P T, Q F: P ∧ Q is F
- P F, Q T: P ∧ Q is F
- P F, Q F: P ∧ Q is F

**Disjunction** (or), written P ∨ Q. True when at least one part (a **disjunct**) is true.
- P T, Q T: P ∨ Q is T
- P T, Q F: P ∨ Q is T
- P F, Q T: P ∨ Q is T
- P F, Q F: P ∨ Q is F

Notice the first row. Logic's "or" is **inclusive**: "You can have cake or ice cream" is true if you have both. English sometimes means the *exclusive* or ("either soup or salad, not both"), which logicians write separately when they need it.

**Conditional** (if-then), written P → Q. P is the **antecedent**, Q the **consequent**. It is false in exactly one case: true antecedent, false consequent.
- P T, Q T: P → Q is T
- P T, Q F: P → Q is F
- P F, Q T: P → Q is T
- P F, Q F: P → Q is T

**Biconditional** (if and only if), written P ↔ Q. True when the parts match.
- P T, Q T: P ↔ Q is T
- P T, Q F: P ↔ Q is F
- P F, Q T: P ↔ Q is F
- P F, Q F: P ↔ Q is T

With two atoms there are 4 rows; with three atoms, 8; in general, n atoms give 2 to the power n rows. That doubling is why truth tables are perfect for short arguments and hopeless, by hand, for long ones.

sections.heading: The Strange Case of the Material Conditional
sections.body:
The last two rows of the conditional table bother almost everyone. They say that if the antecedent is false, "If P then Q" is automatically true. So "If the Moon is made of cheese, then Paris is in France" comes out true. So does "If the Moon is made of cheese, then 2 + 2 = 5." This truth-functional "if" is called the **material conditional**, and its oddities are known as the paradoxes of material implication.

Why accept it? Think of a conditional as a promise. A parent says: "If you finish your homework, you can play video games." When has the parent broken the promise? Only when the child finishes the homework and is *not* allowed to play (row 2). If the child does not finish the homework, the promise simply was not triggered, whatever happens next; it was not broken, so we count it as kept. Given that each row must be either T or F, T is the least bad choice.

A second justification: P → Q has exactly the same truth table as "Either not-P, or Q" (¬P ∨ Q). Check it yourself: ¬P ∨ Q is false only when ¬P is false (P true) and Q is false. That matches row 2 and nothing else.

Still, philosophers disagree about whether the material conditional captures ordinary "if." Counterfactuals like "If Oswald hadn't shot Kennedy, someone else would have" clearly are not truth-functional; their antecedents are false, yet some are true and some false. Philosophers such as Paul Grice argued that the material conditional gives the literal meaning and that the oddness of the cheese sentence comes from conversational expectations (you would mislead a listener by saying it). Others, following Ernest Adams and Dorothy Edgington, think indicative "if" is not a statement with a truth value at all but expresses a conditional probability. You will meet the counterfactual problem again in Lesson 4 on possible worlds. For now, the material conditional is the standard tool, and it does exactly what logic needs: it never lets you get from truth to falsehood.

sections.heading: Validity: The Truth-Table Test
sections.body:
Recall from Day 17 that an argument is **valid** when it is impossible for all the premises to be true and the conclusion false. Validity is about form, not about whether the premises actually are true. A valid argument with true premises is called **sound**.

Truth tables give us a mechanical test. Write out every row. Find the rows where all the premises are true. If the conclusion is true in every one of those rows, the argument is valid. If even one row makes all the premises true and the conclusion false, that row is a **counterexample** and the argument is invalid.

Test the most famous form, **modus ponens** (Latin, roughly "the way of affirming"): P → Q; P; therefore Q.
- Row 1, P T, Q T: premise P → Q is T, premise P is T, conclusion Q is T.
- Row 2, P T, Q F: premise P → Q is F, so this row does not matter.
- Row 3, P F, Q T: premise P is F, so this row does not matter.
- Row 4, P F, Q F: premise P is F, so this row does not matter.

Only row 1 makes both premises true, and there the conclusion is true. Valid.

Now **modus tollens** ("the way of denying"): P → Q; ¬Q; therefore ¬P.
- Row 1, P T, Q T: ¬Q is F. Irrelevant.
- Row 2, P T, Q F: P → Q is F. Irrelevant.
- Row 3, P F, Q T: ¬Q is F. Irrelevant.
- Row 4, P F, Q F: P → Q is T, ¬Q is T, and the conclusion ¬P is T.

Valid again. Modus tollens is the backbone of Popper's falsificationism from Day 72: if the theory is true, the prediction comes out; the prediction did not come out; so the theory is false.

Two more forms worth knowing by name:
- **Disjunctive syllogism**: P ∨ Q; ¬P; therefore Q. ("It's in the kitchen or the car. It's not in the kitchen. So it's in the car.")
- **Hypothetical syllogism**: P → Q; Q → R; therefore P → R. This is a chain of conditionals; it needs an 8-row table because there are three atoms, and you will find no counterexample row.

sections.heading: Two Formal Fallacies and How to Catch Them
sections.body:
A **formal fallacy** is an argument that is invalid because of its form alone, regardless of its subject matter. Two of them are cheap imitations of modus ponens and modus tollens, and they are everywhere.

**Affirming the consequent**: P → Q; Q; therefore P. This is the detective's argument from the opening. Let P be "The butler did it" and Q be "There is mud on his boots."
- Row 1, P T, Q T: premises both T, conclusion T. Fine so far.
- Row 2, P T, Q F: premise P → Q is F. Irrelevant.
- Row 3, P F, Q T: P → Q is T (false antecedent), Q is T, but the conclusion P is F. Counterexample!
- Row 4, P F, Q F: Q is F. Irrelevant.

Row 3 is the world in which the butler is innocent but has muddy boots anyway. Because that world is possible, the argument is invalid.

**Denying the antecedent**: P → Q; ¬P; therefore ¬Q. "If you smoke, you'll damage your lungs. You don't smoke. So your lungs are fine." The counterexample row is again row 3: P false, Q true. You can damage your lungs in other ways, such as air pollution.

Why are these so tempting? One reason is that people often hear "if" as "if and only if." If the parent says "If you finish your homework you can play," the child reasonably infers that *not* finishing means no games, because otherwise why mention the condition? That inference is not licensed by logic but by conversational context. Another reason is that affirming the consequent resembles real scientific reasoning: a theory predicts an observation, the observation occurs, and we gain confidence in the theory. That inference can be reasonable as *evidence* (in probabilistic terms the observation can raise the theory's probability), but it is never deductively valid.

Note carefully: an invalid argument can have a true conclusion. Maybe the butler really did it. The fallacy is not that the conclusion is false, but that the premises fail to guarantee it.

sections.heading: Tautologies, Contradictions and Equivalences
sections.body:
Some compound propositions are true in every row of their truth table, whatever the facts. These are **tautologies**. The simplest is P ∨ ¬P, Aristotle's law of excluded middle from Day 17. Others are false in every row; these are **contradictions**, like P ∧ ¬P, which violates the law of non-contradiction. Everything in between, true in some rows and false in others, is called **contingent**: its truth depends on how the world is. Wittgenstein's *Tractatus* (Day 70) made much of this: tautologies are true come what may, and precisely for that reason, he argued, they say nothing about the world.

There is a neat link between tautologies and validity. An argument with premises A and B and conclusion C is valid exactly when the single conditional (A ∧ B) → C is a tautology. Checking an argument and checking a formula are the same job.

Two propositions are **logically equivalent** when they have the same truth value in every row. Some equivalences are worth memorizing because they untangle everyday confusions:
- **Contraposition**: P → Q is equivalent to ¬Q → ¬P. "If it's a whale, it's a mammal" says the same as "If it's not a mammal, it's not a whale."
- But the **converse**, Q → P, is *not* equivalent. "If it's a mammal, it's a whale" is false. Confusing a conditional with its converse is the root of affirming the consequent.
- **De Morgan's laws**, named after the logician Augustus De Morgan (though known to medieval logicians): ¬(P ∧ Q) is equivalent to ¬P ∨ ¬Q, and ¬(P ∨ Q) is equivalent to ¬P ∧ ¬Q.

De Morgan's laws matter in practice. "It is not the case that the job is both well paid and interesting" means that it is either not well paid or not interesting (or neither). It does *not* mean it is neither.

Finally, a word of caution. Propositional logic is powerful but blunt. It cannot see inside propositions. "All humans are mortal; Socrates is human; so Socrates is mortal" comes out as P; Q; therefore R, which looks invalid, because the validity depends on words like "all" that live inside the atoms. To capture it you need predicate logic, the subject of Lesson 2.

keyQuote.text: Contrariwise, if it was so, it might be; and if it were so, it would be; but as it isn't, it ain't. That's logic.
keyQuote.source: Tweedledee, in Lewis Carroll (a logician by profession), Through the Looking-Glass (1871), Chapter 4

modernConnection.title: Your Phone Is Built Out of Truth Tables
modernConnection.body:
In 1937 a 21-year-old MIT student named Claude Shannon wrote a master's thesis showing that the relay switches in telephone exchanges could be described exactly by Boole's algebra. A switch that is closed is "true"; open is "false." Two switches in series form an AND: current flows only if both are closed. Two switches in parallel form an OR: current flows if either is closed. Shannon realized that any truth table could be built as a circuit, and so any circuit could be designed and simplified with logic. It has been called one of the most important master's theses ever written.

Modern chips are made of billions of tiny transistors arranged into exactly these **logic gates**: AND, OR, NOT, and combinations like NAND (not-and), which is so versatile that every other connective can be built from it alone. When your phone adds two numbers, it is running truth tables at billions of steps per second. Every "if" statement in software is a conditional, and programmers apply De Morgan's laws daily when they rewrite a condition like "not (logged in and verified)."

There is a human twist. In 1966 the psychologist Peter Wason gave people four cards showing E, K, 4 and 7, with a letter on one side and a number on the other, and the rule "If a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other." Which cards must you turn over to test the rule? The correct answer is E and 7 (the 7 could hide a vowel, which would be a true antecedent with a false consequent, the only row that breaks a conditional). In many versions of the experiment, only around ten percent of people get it right; most pick E and 4, which is affirming-the-consequent thinking. Yet when the same structure is framed as a social rule ("If someone is drinking beer, they must be over the legal drinking age"), performance jumps dramatically.

The lesson cuts both ways. Logic is not how human brains spontaneously work, which is exactly why a formal tool is valuable. But context and content shape our reasoning in ways that pure form ignores, which is why psychologists still debate what the Wason task reveals about the mind.

vocabulary.definition: A statement that is either true or false.
vocabulary.example: "Water boils at 100°C at sea level" is a proposition; "Please pass the salt" is not.

vocabulary.definition: A word joining propositions whose compound's truth value depends only on the truth values of its parts.
vocabulary.example: "And" is truth-functional, but "because" is not: two true sentences joined by "because" can still be false.

vocabulary.definition: A systematic list of every combination of truth values for the atomic propositions, showing the value of a compound in each case.
vocabulary.example: A truth table for three atoms has eight rows.

vocabulary.definition: The truth-functional 'if P then Q', false only when P is true and Q is false.
vocabulary.example: On the material conditional, 'If pigs fly, I am the Pope' is true because pigs don't fly.

vocabulary.definition: The property of an argument in which it is impossible for all premises to be true and the conclusion false.
vocabulary.example: Modus tollens is valid even when its premises are false.

vocabulary.definition: The valid form: If P then Q; not Q; therefore not P.
vocabulary.example: If the alarm worked, it would have rung; it didn't ring; so the alarm didn't work.

vocabulary.definition: The invalid form: If P then Q; Q; therefore P.
vocabulary.example: If it rained, the lawn is wet; the lawn is wet; so it rained (ignoring the sprinkler).

vocabulary.definition: A compound proposition true in every row of its truth table, true by form alone.
vocabulary.example: 'Either it will snow tomorrow or it won't' is a tautology and tells you nothing about the weather.

thinkingExercise.title: Build the Table, Catch the Fallacy
thinkingExercise.prompt: Take one argument you have heard recently (from the news, a debate, an advertisement or a family dinner) that uses 'if' and test it formally.
steps: Write the argument as plainly as possible in premises and conclusion. Assign letters (P, Q, maybe R) to the simple statements.
Translate it into symbols using ¬, ∧, ∨, → and ↔.
Write out the full truth table as a list of rows, marking for each row the value of every premise and the conclusion.
Decide: is there any row where all premises are true and the conclusion false? If so, describe in words the real-world situation that row represents.
If the argument is invalid, ask whether it could still be reasonable as evidence for its conclusion, and write two sentences explaining the difference between 'valid' and 'good evidence'.

summary: Propositional logic studies how whole statements combine using truth-functional connectives; it was first developed by the Stoics, especially Chrysippus, and revived by Boole and Frege.

The five connectives (not, and, or, if-then, if-and-only-if) each have a fixed truth table; logical 'or' is inclusive and the material conditional is false only when the antecedent is true and the consequent false.
An argument is valid if no row of its truth table makes all premises true and the conclusion false; such a row is a counterexample.
Modus ponens, modus tollens, disjunctive syllogism and hypothetical syllogism are valid; affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent are formal fallacies.

Tautologies are true in every row, and equivalences such as contraposition and De Morgan's laws help untangle everyday reasoning, but propositional logic cannot see inside sentences to words like 'all' and 'some'.

quiz.question: In which single case is the material conditional P → Q false?
quiz.explanation: A conditional is broken only when the antecedent holds and the consequent fails. With a false antecedent the conditional counts as true.

quiz.question: 'If the theory is correct, the experiment will show a shift. The experiment showed a shift. So the theory is correct.' This argument is:
options: Valid, because it is modus ponens
Valid, because it is modus tollens
quiz.explanation: It moves from 'If P then Q' and 'Q' to 'P', which is affirming the consequent. The observation may be evidence for the theory, but it does not deductively guarantee it.

quiz.question: Logical 'or' (∨) is false when both disjuncts are true.
quiz.explanation: Logical disjunction is inclusive: P ∨ Q is true when at least one disjunct is true, including when both are.

quiz.question: How many rows does a truth table need for an argument containing four different atomic propositions?
quiz.explanation: Each atom doubles the rows: 2 to the power 4 is 16.

quiz.question: Which proposition is logically equivalent to 'If it's a square, it has four sides'?
options: If it doesn't have four sides, it isn't a square
If it has four sides, it's a square
If it isn't a square, it doesn't have four sides
It's a square and it has four sides
quiz.explanation: The contrapositive (not-Q → not-P) is equivalent to the original. The second option is the converse and the third is the inverse; neither is equivalent.

quiz.question: An invalid argument can have a true conclusion.
quiz.explanation: Invalidity means the premises fail to guarantee the conclusion, not that the conclusion is false. The butler might really have done it.

quiz.question: By De Morgan's laws, 'It is not true that the hotel is cheap and central' is equivalent to:
options: The hotel is neither cheap nor central
The hotel is not cheap or it is not central
The hotel is cheap but not central
The hotel is central but not cheap
quiz.explanation: ¬(P ∧ Q) is equivalent to ¬P ∨ ¬Q. It allows that one of the two could still be true, so 'neither' is too strong.

quiz.question: Which ancient thinker is usually credited with the first systematic logic of 'if', 'and' and 'or' propositions?
quiz.explanation: Aristotle's syllogistic dealt with categorical terms; the Stoics, especially Chrysippus, developed the logic of compound propositions.

quiz.question: An argument is valid exactly when the conditional 'if (all premises) then (conclusion)' is a tautology.
quiz.explanation: If no row makes all premises true and the conclusion false, then that conditional is true in every row, which is what being a tautology means.

quiz.question: In the Wason selection task (cards E, K, 4, 7; rule: 'if vowel, then even number'), which cards must be turned over?
quiz.explanation: Only a vowel paired with an odd number would break the rule. So check E (could have an odd number) and 7 (could have a vowel). The 4 is irrelevant: whatever is behind it, the rule survives.

goDeeper.body:
Truth tables are a **semantic** method: they check validity by surveying all possible assignments of truth values. Logicians also build **proof systems**, sets of rules like modus ponens that let you derive conclusions step by step without looking at truth values at all. The deep question is whether the two match. For propositional logic they do: the system is **sound** (every provable argument is valid) and **complete** (every valid argument is provable). Emil Post proved a version of completeness for propositional logic in his 1921 dissertation.

A second question is about efficiency. Checking a truth table with n atoms takes 2 to the power n rows, which explodes quickly; 60 atoms would take longer than the age of the universe at a billion rows per second. Is there a fundamentally faster method for deciding whether a formula can be made true? This is the satisfiability problem (SAT). In 1971 Stephen Cook showed that SAT is NP-complete, meaning that a fast general method for it would give fast methods for a huge range of hard problems. Whether one exists is the famous P versus NP question, one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's million-dollar Millennium Prize problems. In practice, modern SAT solvers handle formulas with millions of variables using clever heuristics, and they are used to verify computer chips and plan logistics.

Finally, not every logician accepts the classical truth tables. Intuitionists, following L. E. J. Brouwer, reject the general validity of excluded middle (P ∨ ¬P) for mathematics, insisting that a proof of a disjunction requires a proof of one disjunct. Relevance logicians reject the paradoxes of material implication, demanding that the antecedent of a valid conditional actually be relevant to its consequent.

questions: Is the material conditional a good analysis of the English word 'if', or merely a useful substitute? What would be lost if logic used a different conditional?
Wittgenstein said tautologies say nothing. Yet mathematics and logic seem to teach us a great deal. How could both be true?
If most people fail the Wason task, what does that tell us about whether logic describes how we think or how we ought to think?
